opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think those stories get passed around in a way that flattens what's actually going on. I don't have firsthand knowledge of any specific meeting, so I can't vouch for the details of who got fired or why. But the pattern people describe, extremely blunt reviews and very little patience for vague answers, fits how Elon has run most of his companies.

My read is this. Humanoid robotics is a field where it's very easy to make a beautiful demo and very hard to make something that works reliably, cheaply, and at scale. If you're running a project like Optimus, the biggest risk isn't that people aren't smart. It's that the organization slowly drifts into polishing demos, writing nice slides, and hedging every estimate. Elon's style is basically a brute-force correction for that. He pushes on first principles: why does this actuator cost this much, why does this take six months, who exactly owns this number? If someone can't answer, he treats that as a signal about the organization, not just the person.

Is that the best way to manage people? I have mixed feelings. On one hand, the intensity creates enormous clarity and speed. Everyone knows the bar, decisions get made fast, and you don't get the slow bureaucratic bloat that kills a lot of big-company robotics efforts. On the other hand, robotics research has real uncertainty. Sometimes the honest answer is "we don't know yet," and if that answer is punished, people learn to give confident answers instead of true ones. That can be dangerous, especially when you're dealing with things like learning-based control, where progress is nonlinear and hard to predict.

So I'd frame it as a trade-off. Tesla is betting that manufacturing discipline, vertical integration, and a very aggressive culture can turn humanoids into a product the way they turned EVs into a product. That culture is great at execution and cost-down. Whether it's equally good at the open-ended research parts of the problem, like general manipulation and generalization to new environments, is the open question. My guess is the companies that win in humanoids will need both: Tesla-level execution pressure, plus enough psychological safety that researchers can say "this approach isn't working" early, without fearing for their jobs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses execution risks and organizational pressure, but does not suggest reported firings happen when projects face existential stakes.

r002.rationale: It describes pressure for answers and mixed feelings about the management style, but does not distinguish pressure on project leaders from impatience with the humanoid project overall.

r003.rationale: It recognizes robotics research is uncertain, but does not connect Musk’s patience with the project to that uncertainty; it instead describes little patience for vague answers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll say up front that I don't know the inside details of those specific firing stories, so I'll talk about the pattern rather than any particular incident.

What I think people miss is that Musk runs Optimus the way he runs everything, which is by compressing the distance between himself and the engineering reality. When he sits in a review and someone can't explain why a joint actuator is behind schedule, or gives a vague answer about tendon durability in the hand, he treats that as a signal that the person doesn't actually own the problem. The firing stories, whether exaggerated or not, come out of that culture. He wants the person in the room to be the one who can answer the physics question, not a manager relaying someone else's slide.

There's a real upside to that. Humanoid robots are an absurdly hard integration problem. Hands, batteries, actuators, perception, the training pipeline, all of it has to converge at once, and traditional program management tends to let each group hide behind interfaces and schedules. The Tesla approach forces people to confront the hard parts early, and it's why they've iterated through hardware generations faster than most robotics labs would dare.

But the cost is obvious too. If people are afraid of being the one who delivers bad news, you lose the honest signal you need most on a project this uncertain. Fear is good at making people work harder on known problems. It's bad at surfacing unknown ones. And a humanoid program is almost entirely unknown problems. So I think it's less a story about one man's temper and more a bet that velocity and accountability matter more than psychological safety at this stage. Whether that bet pays off depends on whether the people who survive that environment are the ones who actually understand the machine, or just the ones who are good at surviving reviews.

r001.rationale: The response describes technical difficulty and uncertainty, but does not suggest that reported firings occur when the project faces existential stakes.

r002.rationale: It attributes pressure to accountability and engineering reviews, but does not distinguish pressure on project leaders from impatience with the overall undertaking.

r003.rationale: It recognizes the project’s technical uncertainty, but does not connect that uncertainty to Musk’s patience with humanoid robotics.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate those stories from what we can actually conclude about the project. A story about someone being fired during a report doesn’t tell us what led up to it, whether the report exposed a deeper problem, or even how accurately the incident was described.

But it raises a real management question: can people bring bad news to the person making decisions? With a humanoid robot, you’re dealing with difficult engineering problems and a lot of uncertainty. You want ambitious targets and clear accountability, but you also need engineers to say, “This isn’t working, and here’s why.” If people think that admission could get them fired, the risk is that reports become more optimistic while the underlying problems stay unresolved.

So I’d judge Musk’s management less by the dramatic anecdotes and more by whether the team can surface problems honestly, learn from failures, and demonstrate progress. Pressure can create urgency. It can’t replace accurate information.

r002.rationale: It discusses pressure and accountability generally, without distinguishing pressure on project leaders from impatience with the overall undertaking.

r003.rationale: It notes the project has difficult engineering problems and uncertainty, but does not connect Musk’s patience with robotics to recognizing that uncertainty.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the stories from what we can actually conclude. A story about someone being fired during a report doesn’t, by itself, tell us how Elon manages Tesla’s humanoid robot project. You’d need to know what happened, what expectations had been set, and whether this was an isolated incident or a pattern.

But the management tension is real: you want urgency and accountability, while also making it safe for engineers to report bad news. With a project this uncertain, people have to be able to say, “This isn’t working, and here’s what we learned.” If they’re afraid that admitting a problem will cost them their job, you risk getting reassuring reports instead of useful information. So I’d judge the approach by whether it produces honest feedback and sustained technical progress, rather than by how dramatic the stories sound.
